abstract: The lymphatic vasculature returns interstitial fluid to the blood circulation, a function that depends on rhythmic contraction of the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) surrounding collecting vessels. Lymph transport declines with age, a decline attributed largely to loss of SMCs from collecting vessels. We show that the principal change is not their loss but the loss of their contractile phenotype. In mouse ear collecting vessels, contractile protein expression declined with age and the vessels dilated, yet the majority of SMCs remained on the vessel wall. The decline extended to serum response factor (SRF), the transcription factor driving the smooth muscle contractile gene programme, and was mirrored by a loss of SRF-dependent contractile transcripts in published single-cell data from aged lymphatic muscle cells. Inducible deletion of Srf in mural cells reproduced this state, abolishing the contractile programme while leaving the cells in place and thereby excluding impaired SMC recruitment as the main mechanism. The resulting vessels became severely dilated and misshapen, whereas lymphatic capillaries were unaffected; endothelial identity, valve formation and lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) number were all preserved, with enlargement instead reflecting increased LEC size. Intravital imaging showed loss of both rhythmic contraction and the contractile movement of individual SMCs, and Evans blue drainage to the inguinal lymph node was correspondingly reduced. Deletion of Srf after the contractile phenotype was established recapitulated this loss, showing that SRF is required continuously to maintain lymphatic SMC contractility and providing a genetic model of age-associated lymphatic dysfunction.
